## Overview of the Enriched Pathways

In Table 1, we rank the enriched biological pathways associated with heart failure based on statistical significance, biological coherence, and relevance to disease mechanisms. Notably, extracellular matrix organization (Reactome:R-HSA-1474244, p < 4.77 × 10−22), external encapsulating structure (Gene Ontology:0030312, p < 4.28 × 10−48), glycosaminoglycan binding (Gene Ontology:0005539, p < 1.28 × 10−15), endopeptidase activity (Gene Ontology:0004175, p < 7.23 × 10−14), and Cell adhesion molecules (Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes:04514, p < 1.28 × 10−8) collectively point to extensive extracellular matrix remodeling, altered cell-matrix interactions, and proteolytic turnover. These processes are central features of cardiac fibrosis and adverse ventricular remodeling in heart failure, and substantial literature has shown that dysregulated collagen deposition, matrix metalloproteinase activity, and altered adhesion signaling contribute directly to myocardial stiffening, chamber dilation, and progressive contractile dysfunction.

Furthermore, strong enrichment of immune and inflammatory pathways, including Cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction (Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes:04060, p < 3.43 × 10−44), humoral immune response (Gene Ontology:0006959, p < 7.56 × 10−20), Neutrophil degranulation (Reactome:R-HSA-6798695, p < 4.51 × 10−12), antigen processing and presentation (Gene Ontology:0019882, p < 4.88 × 10−7), receptor complex (Gene Ontology:0043235, p < 6.48 × 10−17), and Allograft rejection (WikiPathways:2328, p < 3.64 × 10−8), supports a major role for innate and adaptive immune activation in heart failure. This is consistent with evidence that inflammatory cytokines, leukocyte recruitment, antigen presentation, and antibody-mediated responses promote cardiomyocyte injury, endothelial dysfunction, and fibrotic remodeling, particularly in chronic heart failure and inflammatory cardiomyopathies.

In addition, the enrichment of Amyloidosis (Human Phenotype Ontology:0011034, p < 8.08 × 10−4) is highly relevant because amyloid deposition is a well-established cause of restrictive cardiomyopathy and heart failure, especially in transthyretin- and immunoglobulin-related cardiac amyloidosis. Although terms such as Intracranial hemorrhage (Human Phenotype Ontology:0002170, p < 1.12 × 10−2), Pleural mesothelioma (WikiPathways:5087, p < 6.05 × 10−5), and tissue-enriched signatures from Colon; goblet cells[greater than or equal to Low] (Human Protein Atlas:0130891, p < 4.11 × 10−5) and Colon; endocrine cells[greater than or equal to Low] (Human Protein Atlas:0131291, p < 5.88 × 10−5) are less heart-specific, they may reflect shared secretory, inflammatory, extracellular, or protease-related programs rather than direct cardiac pathology. Overall, the highly significant p-values and the convergence of matrix remodeling, immune activation, adhesion signaling, and amyloid-associated biology strongly support these pathways as plausible contributors to the pathogenesis and progression of heart failure.
